full_judgment:
2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, that the present opposite party No. 1 as pre-emptor instituted the original Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case being No. 60 of 2003 in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dakop, Khulna under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 contending inter alia that the case joie appertaining to Mouza Dhopadihi under S.A. khatian No. 63 ad 68 comprising an area of .99 acres of land originally belonged to one Kali Charan Sarder in 08 annas share who died leaving behind his two sons Ajit Sarder and Jagadish Sarder. Ajit Sarder subsequently purchased 61/2 decimals of land on 24.05.1983 from the case holding. The pre-emptor by a sub-kabala deed dated 12.07.1977 purchased 50 decimals of land from Jagadish in the case holding and by virtue of this purchase he became a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding. At the demise of Ajit Sarder, his two sons the opposite party No. 3 and 4 became the heirs and the opposite party No. 2 behind the back of the pre-emptor transferred 99 decimals of land in favour of the purchaser-opposite party No. 1 who is a stranger purchaser to the case jote. The pre-emptor initially by a bainapatra acquired 49 decimals of land from the opposite party No. 3 and finally through a decree of a specific performance of contract in Suit No. 103 of 2000 he got the transfer deed registered. The further case of the pre-emptor is such that the pre-emptor for the time came to learn about the case kabala through her husband on 04.08.2003 and after getting the certified copy of the kabala on 07.08.2003 filed the original pre-emption miscellaneous case for getting the case land pre-empted. 

 9. As against the aforesaid submission of the learned counsel for the petitioner, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 opposing the Rule controverted the argument advanced from the side of the petitioner and submits that, neither the trial court nor the Appellate Court during disposal of the original pre-emption miscellaneous case and its subsequent appeal committed any illegality or irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned courts below in their judgment and orders after proper analysis of evidence in its true perspective and appreciation of law concurrently held that the pre-emptor-opposite party is a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding and she has locus standi to file the original case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and accordingly she filed the case within time and in that case there is no defect of party. The learned Advocate also submits that the learned Appellate Court in deciding the merit of the appeal rightly held in the findings and decision that the pre-emptee-appellant claiming her status in the case holding as co-sharer by purchase did not file any application for ratable pre-emption under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 within time and for the said reason there is no scope to consider her case as to the relief of ratable pre-emption from the side of the pre-emptee-appellant. The learned Advocate lastly submits that it is in the evidence that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding and there is no legal embargo from her side to get the case land pre-empted and apart from this, there is no misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and order can be interfered with. 

 11. Having gone through the case records it transpires that admittedly the pre-emptor-opposite party is a co-sharer in the case holding and the transfer was done by one of the co-sharer of the case jote in favour of the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1. There is no paper to show that any notice under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was served upon the co-sharers of the case jote prior to transfer of the land and it is also apparent from the face of the papers that on 19.06.2003 the transfer was held against which the pre-emptor instituted the original pre-emption miscellaneous case on 14.10.2003. Hence; the case was instituted within time. Furthermore, it is apparent that at the time of institution of the case, the case kabala was not registered under section 60 of the Registration Act and during pendency of the case the registration was completed. Therefore; the learned court below was justified in holding the view that the case is not time barred and not premature before disposal. Secondly; in the instant case obviously it is the concurrent observation and findings of both the courts below that the case is not bad for defect of parties. 

 16. Scrutinizing the relevant papers along with the evidences on record it appears that, admittedly the pre-emptor acquired some land by purchase in the case holding and the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1 also claimed that she is a co-sharer by purchase with same status by virtue of a kabala deed dated 29.08.1985. But the fact remains that by dint of Exhibit-`Gha' the opposite party, who is the petitioner to the present case despite of claiming herself a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding, but during pendency of the case using this status as a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding with that of the pre-emptor, did not take any step by filing any application under sub-section (4) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for ratable pre-emption under the prescribed rules as incorporated in the relevant provision of law and the learned Appellate Court was quite justified in holding the view that, save and except such prayer for ratable pre-emption under the ambit of law there is no scope to consider her case. On the other hand, for similar status of the pre-emptee with that of the pre-emptor, the case of the pre-emptor-opposite party to the present case is not barred.
